2027-04-09.title: Second Friday of Resurrection
2027-04-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-04-09.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. On Fridays the Church remembers the Passion of the Lord; in the Easter season it remembers it in the light of the Resurrection.
2027-04-09.verse: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
theo: Every Friday is a little Good Friday, and on this Friday of the Easter season Paul brings us back to the Cross. Corinth was a city that admired clever speakers and new ideas. Into that world Paul brought a message that sounded absurd: that the Saviour of the world was a man executed on a Roman cross, the death reserved for slaves and rebels. “For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Paul does not soften the scandal. He quotes Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.” Then he asks: “Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” Human wisdom, for all its brilliance, did not find its way to God. So “God decided, through the foolishness of our proclamation, to save those who believe.” The Cross is not a clever argument that wins debates; it is an act of love that saves. After Easter we know that the Crucified is alive, and that is why the Cross is the power of God: the weakest moment in history became the moment death was defeated.

Paul describes the two ways people resist this message. Some want signs, proofs of power; others want wisdom, a philosophy that satisfies the mind. “But we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Paul himself was a Jew, and the first to receive this message in Jerusalem were Jews; he is describing not a people but a temptation found in every human heart, which wants God to prove himself on our terms. Our own age asks for both: give us miracles on demand, give us arguments we can control. God gives instead a crucified and risen Lord. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala have long venerated the Cross without the figure of the Body, the Cross of the Resurrection, glorious because the Lord is risen; the Mar Thoma Cross with its flowering arms and the dove above shows the tree of death become the tree of life. The Cross is not the end of Christ's story but the door to Easter.

In the Gospel Jesus sits in a boat and teaches the crowd on the shore. “Listen! A sower went out to sow.” The seed falls on four kinds of ground: the hard path where birds snatch it, the rocky ground where it springs up and withers, the thorns that choke it, and the good soil where it yields “thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.” Jesus himself is the sower, and his word is the seed. The parable is honest: much of the sowing seems wasted. Yet the sower keeps sowing, generously, even on the path, because the harvest in the good soil is beyond all calculation. The two readings belong together. The Cross itself looked like seed thrown away: a life buried in the ground. Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Easter is that harvest. The question the parable leaves with us is not about the sower but about the soil: what kind of ground does the word find in me? “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
conn: Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14: “The wisdom of their wise shall perish, and the discernment of the discerning shall be hidden.”
“For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).
“But he was wounded for our transgressions… and by his bruises we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).
The word that does not return empty.
“So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11).
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).
In Luke the good soil are those who “hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance” (Luke 8:15).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present, not repeated: the Lord who was crucified offers himself to the Father, and the Risen Lord gives himself to us as food.
The word sown in the readings and the Bread broken at the altar are one gift: the seed that died and rose, now bearing fruit in those who receive him.

live: Spend five minutes today before a crucifix or the Mar Thoma Cross and thank the Lord for his love.
Name one ‘thorn’ that chokes God's word in you, such as worry or a screen habit, and cut it back this week.
Share a Gospel verse with someone this week, without worrying about the result.
Read Mark 4:1–20 at home and ask which ground you are today.
fathers: The Cross won the world, and through unlearned men. Fishermen and tentmakers persuaded philosophers and kings; men without eloquence overcame the orators. This is the clearest sign that the Cross is the power of God: it did not need human wisdom, and it conquered all of it.

The good soil brings forth fruit through patience. Whatever good we do is nothing unless we bear patiently the evils done to us by our neighbour. The seed that falls in the good earth must endure the winter before it rises in the harvest.
magis: Faith in God's almighty power is put to the test by evil and suffering; but in the Resurrection of Christ, God has shown the immeasurable greatness of his power: Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
It is love to the end that gives Christ's sacrifice its value as redemption and reparation.
The word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and join the little flock of Christ have welcomed the Kingdom.
The Church urges all the faithful to learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ by frequent reading of the divine Scriptures, accompanied by prayer.
saints: Monday 5 to Saturday 10 April: the second week of the Resurrection. Sunday 11 April: the Third Sunday of Resurrection. The Latin Church keeps the Annunciation of the Lord on Monday 5 April this year (moved from 25 March, which fell on Pesaha Thursday); Syro-Malabar faithful follow the direction of their eparchy.
2027-04-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, the message of your Cross is foolishness to the world but to us the power of God. Keep us from demanding signs on our own terms and from trusting only our own wisdom. You are the sower who goes out to sow: make our hearts good soil, clear away the stones and thorns, and let your word bear fruit in us, thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

2027-04-09.question: What kind of ground does God's word find in me today?
catechism: The power of God in the Cross.
kidsaint: St Alphonsa of Bharananganam was often sick and in pain. Instead of complaining, she offered her sufferings to Jesus with love, like a seed planted in the ground. Today she is the first woman saint of India, and many people pray at her tomb. Lesson: when we offer even our hurts to Jesus, he can make them grow into something beautiful!
term: From the Greek parabolē, ‘something placed beside’: a short story from ordinary life placed beside the mystery of God's Kingdom to help us understand it. Jesus' parables invite the listener to decide; that is why he ends, “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”

family.explain: A farmer threw seeds everywhere. Some fell on the path and birds ate them. Some fell on rocks and dried up. Some fell among thorns and got choked. But some fell on good soil and grew into a big harvest! Jesus says God's word is like seed. When we listen and keep it in our hearts, it grows.
family.intention: We pray for farmers, and for all who teach God's word to children.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we make our hearts good soil for Jesus' word this week?”

illus: A Sunday school teacher in a hill parish in Idukki taught catechism for over forty years. She sometimes said that most of her pupils forgot everything the week after their Confirmation, and she wondered if her work was worth it. In her eightieth year a letter came from a priest working among tribal villages in Madhya Pradesh. He had been the noisiest boy in her class, the one she had once sent out of the room. ‘You told us that the seed is never wasted,’ he wrote. ‘I did not listen then. But it stayed in me. Today I baptised thirty-two people. This harvest is yours too.’ She kept the letter in her Bible until she died.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, crucified and risen, sow your word in our hearts now, and make them good soil. Amen. Alleluia!
share: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing (1 Corinthians 1:18). Do I ever feel embarrassed by the Cross?
Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Where do I look for power and wisdom apart from Christ?
Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it (Mark 4:7). What thorns choke God's word in me?
Thirty and sixty and a hundredfold (Mark 4:8). What fruit is the Lord asking of me this Easter?
pm.resp: Lord, make us good soil for your word.
interc: For preachers and catechists, that they may sow the word generously without losing heart.
For those who find the Cross foolish, that they may discover in it the power and love of God.
For farmers in Kerala and throughout India, for good rains and a just reward for their labour.
For those whose faith is choked by worry or wealth, that they may make room for God again.
For the Church in North India and all mission lands, that the seed of the Gospel may bear a hundredfold.
pm.close: Father, in the foolishness of the Cross you revealed your power and wisdom, and in the Resurrection you brought forth the harvest. Make our hearts good soil, and let your word bear fruit in us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, every Friday is a little Good Friday, even in the Easter season. Today Paul says: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
In Corinth people admired clever speakers. Paul preached a Saviour who died on a cross. It sounded absurd. But God chose the foolishness of the Cross to save those who believe.

Some want signs on demand; some want wisdom they can control. We proclaim Christ crucified, the power of God and the wisdom of God. And because he is risen, the Cross is no longer a sign of defeat. Our Mar Thoma Cross flowers at its ends: the tree of death has become the tree of life.
In the Gospel Jesus tells of a sower who throws seed everywhere: on the path, on rock, among thorns, and on good soil. Much seems wasted, yet the good soil yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.

Jesus is the sower, and his word is the seed. The Cross itself looked like a seed thrown away, but it rose in the Easter harvest. The question is about us: what kind of ground does his word find in me?
This week, let us clear away one thorn, and let the word take root. Let anyone with ears to hear listen! Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about a farmer who threw seeds. Some were eaten by birds, some dried up, some got choked by thorns, but some grew into a big harvest!
God's word is like a seed. When you listen to Bible stories and remember them, the seed grows in your heart.
